::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A provocative paper, on purpose.** A thesis, a model, a simulation and predictions that could prove it wrong. It follows [Stop Reviewing Pull Requests](../2026-10-23-stop-reviewing-pull-requests/index.qmd), which let go of approving each change; this one lets go of the testing layers around a feature *while it is being built*. Figures 1 and 2 are schematics of my own; Figures 3 and 4 and Table 2 come from [sim.py](sim.py) and [figs.py](figs.py). The parameters are chosen, not measured.
:::

**Abstract.** The standard advice is to *shift left*: test earlier and more, before anyone uses the software. When agents write the code, the defects that survive unit tests are mostly defects of *fit*: the code does what was asked, but not what the domain needs. Integration suites, end-to-end tests and QA passes rarely catch these, and while a feature is still changing they cost time in every cycle. I propose two phases. **Develop:** unit tests and automatic checks only, deploy to production behind a flag, let domain experts use each version in their real work, fix overnight. **Lock in:** when the feature is accepted, generate the regression suite and extra unit tests from the behaviour the experts approved, automate them, then flip the flag. A simple model shows that a suite run in every cycle pays only if $s/T < \ln(1-e\varphi)/\ln(1-q)$, which with plausible values means less than about four hours per cycle. In a simulation, develop-then-lock-in reaches the market in 7 days instead of 13, with the same number of escaped defects and an eighth of the engineering time. Existing features keep a fully automated regression suite on every build. I give the conditions and five predictions that would prove the thesis wrong.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Claims

1. **The rule.** While a feature is being built: unit tests, automatic checks, a flag, and domain experts using it every day. When it is done: lock it in with a generated, automated regression suite, then flip the flag.
2. **Why.** With agents, most defects that remain are about fit, and only people who know the domain see them. A suite written for a moving feature mostly tests behaviour that will change.
3. **The condition.** A suite run in every cycle pays only if $s/T < \ln(1-e\varphi)/\ln(1-q)$. As agents improve, $\varphi$ falls and the bound goes to zero.
4. **Existing features.** They are protected by a fully automated regression suite that runs on every build. Nothing in this proposal touches it.
5. **The test.** Features built this way should reach the market sooner, with no more escaped defects and no more regressions. If they do not, the thesis is wrong.
:::

## 1. Introduction

My thesis: **while a new feature is being developed, the testing layers between the unit test and the user should go.** That means integration and end-to-end suites written as the feature evolves, manual test plans, QA passes, staging as a gate and acceptance at the end. They should not shrink. They should go, until the feature is done.

Every day I see agents write in an hour what used to take a week. What has not sped up is learning whether what was built is right. That knowledge belongs to the people who use the software: application engineers, specialists, experienced internal users. In an afternoon they find what no test plan foresaw, because they know what the software is *for*. The usual process puts them last. Each finding they make then goes back through every layer (Figure 1, top).

The proposal turns this around (Figure 1, bottom). The agent writes the change with its unit tests, the checks run, and the change goes to production behind a flag: off for customers, on for a few domain experts. They use it that day, their findings go to the agent in the evening, and a new version is ready the next morning. When a day or two go by with nothing new, the feature is done. Only then do we write the full regression suite, against behaviour that no longer moves. Then we flip the flag.

## 2. Background

**Shift left.** Testing early rests on the claim that a defect costs one to two orders of magnitude more to fix the later it is found [@boehm1981]. The evidence for that curve is thinner than its fame [@bossavit2015], and agile practice argued that short iterations flatten it [@beck1999]. *Shift-left testing* named the practice of moving tests earlier [@smith2001], and the *test pyramid* gave it a shape: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few end-to-end tests [@cohn2009].

**Deploy is not release.** Continuous delivery showed that small, frequent releases are both faster and safer [@humble2010; @forsgren2018]. Large web companies deploy many times a day and decide separately, with flags, when a feature is *released* [@feitelson2013; @savor2016]. Flags have known costs: more paths through the code, and flags that must be removed [@rahman2016; @hodgson2017]. Staged rollouts and automatic rollback limit the damage of a bad build [@beyer2016].

**Learning from use.** Using one's own software before customers do is an old practice [@harrison2006]. *Build, measure, learn* treats each release as an experiment [@ries2011], and controlled experiments made that rigorous at scale [@kohavi2020].

**Locking in behaviour.** *Characterization tests* record what a system does today so that later changes cannot alter it unnoticed [@feathers2004]. Regression suites are then selected and prioritised so they run fast on every change [@yoo2012; @memon2017]. Language models now generate useful unit tests [@schafer2024], and at Meta they improve existing test suites in production use [@alshahwan2024]. Writing the suite has become cheap. Deciding what the right behaviour is has not.

## 3. A model of the development loop

A feature is built in cycles of length $T$, here one working day. Defects come in two kinds. *Implementation defects*: the code does not do what was specified, which a machine can detect. *Fit defects*: the code does what was specified, but not what the domain needs, which only someone who knows the domain notices, usually while using it.

Let $\varphi$ be the share of implementation defects among those left. Experts using the feature in place find a share $q$ of the remaining defects each cycle. An engineering-side suite adds $s$ to each cycle and catches a share $e$ of implementation defects, but almost no fit defects, because it is written from the same specification as the code. Without the suite, remaining defects are multiplied by $(1-q)$ every $T$. With it, by roughly $(1-q)(1-e\varphi)$ every $T+s$. The suite speeds up learning when

$$
\frac{\ln(1-q) + \ln(1-e\varphi)}{T + s} < \frac{\ln(1-q)}{T}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{s}{T} < \frac{\ln(1-e\varphi)}{\ln(1-q)} .
$$ {#eq-suite}

In plain words: *the suite must cost a smaller share of the cycle than the share of learning it adds.* With $e = 0.6$, half the defects of each kind and experts who find half of what remains each day, the bound is about $0.51$: under four hours in an eight-hour cycle.

**What agents change.** $T$ shrinks, so the fixed cost $s$ becomes a large part of each cycle. And $\varphi$ falls: agents with unit tests increasingly write code that does what it is told, so most remaining mistakes are in what it was told. As $\varphi \to 0$, the bound goes to zero. *Assumption F: for features built by agents with unit tests, most defects that survive the unit tests are fit defects.* Prediction H3 tests it.

**Why $s$ is large while a feature moves.** The cost of a suite is not its run time. It is writing tests for behaviour that changes every day, rewriting them when it does, rerunning flaky ones [@luo2014], and having a person decide, for each failure, whether the code or the test is wrong. Figure 2 shows the effect: during development, most effort on higher-level tests goes into behaviour that will change. Once the feature is accepted, its behaviour stops moving, and the same tests are written once and stay valid.

**What a flag changes.** We used to catch everything before release because a defect reaching customers caused harm. Behind a flag, a defect an expert finds hurts no customer: it is reported, and the next version fixes it. The flag removes most of the harm that made early testing worth its cost.

## 4. The rule in practice

**Developing a new feature.** Before production: the build, types and linters, static analysis, dependency and security scans, and the unit tests the agent writes for each changed behaviour. No test is deleted or weakened without a recorded decision, as in the previous paper. These checks run in minutes and keep $\varphi$ low. After that, the feature goes to production behind a flag. Three to five domain experts use it in their real work, an hour or two a day, and write down what they find in a short form the agent can read. Where possible, the agent turns each finding into a unit test.

**Done: lock it in.** When the experts go two days without a new finding, the feature is done. Behaviour is now stable, and that is the right moment to test it in depth. The agent generates the regression suite from the accepted behaviour: characterization tests [@feathers2004] taken from the experts' recorded sessions, end-to-end scenarios for the main paths, and extra unit tests for the edge cases the experts found. These tests encode what the experts approved, not what the specification said. A person checks that the suite covers what matters, and from then on it runs automatically on every build. Then the flag is flipped, in stages: experts, then a pilot group, then everyone, watching errors and latency [@beyer2016; @kohavi2020]. Afterwards the flag and the old path are removed [@rahman2016].

**Existing features.** Everything already in the market is protected by its automated regression suite, which runs on every build and is selected and prioritised to stay fast [@yoo2012; @memon2017]. This is not optional and not manual. A new feature under development changes shared code too, and that is where regressions come from. The suite is what lets the experts' loop move fast without breaking what customers already rely on. A failure in it blocks the build like a failing unit test.

**What stays in every phase.** Staged rollout and automatic rollback for every build. The thin gate from the previous paper for what cannot be undone: a flag does not make a deleted table or a sent payment reversible. And where a domain requires formal quality control or validation, it happens once, at lock-in, on the build that will be released. The loop does not replace QC. It fills the gap before it, with the part of quality that only use reveals.

## 5. A simulation

I simulated one feature under five policies. It starts with twelve defects, half of each kind, and every fix has some chance of adding a new one. The full suite costs one working day per cycle. It catches 60% of the remaining implementation defects and 10% of the fit defects. Experts find 60% and 40% respectively each day. Lock-in is the same suite run once, in one day, after acceptance. The parameters (Table 1) are chosen, not measured, and generous to the suite.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Defects in the first version | 12, $\varphi = 0.5$ |
| Cycle without suite, $T$ | 1 working day |
| Suite per cycle, $s$ | 1 working day, 4 engineer hours (2 h in Figure 3) |
| Lock-in | the same suite once, 1 day, 4 engineer hours |
| Unit tests and checks catch | 50% of new implementation defects |
| Suite catches, $e$ | 60% of implementation, 10% of fit defects |
| Experts find per day | 60% of implementation, 40% of fit defects |
| Chance a fix adds a defect | 15% |
| Done when | 2 days in a row with nothing found (1 to 5 in Figure 3) |
| Runs | 4 000 per policy |

: **Table 1.** Simulation parameters. *Shift left* runs the suite until it finds nothing, then hands over to experts; each finding goes back through the suite. The other policies test in place from day one.

| Policy | Days to market (p90) | Left for customers | Suite hours | Expert hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shift left | 13.2 (17.8) | 0.39 | 30 | 10.5 |
| Suite + flag | 12.0 (16.0) | 0.33 | 24 | 11.8 |
| Unit tests + flag | 6.0 (9.0) | 0.47 | 0 | 12.9 |
| **Unit tests + flag + lock-in (proposed)** | **7.0 (9.1)** | **0.39** | **4** | 12.8 |
| No tests + flag | 7.0 (9.0) | 0.46 | 0 | 13.9 |

: **Table 2.** Simulation results for one feature: median days to market (90th percentile), defects left for customers, engineer hours on the suite, and expert hours. Standard errors are 0.01 or less for defects left. Run `python sim.py` to reproduce them.

**The proposal reaches the market in about half the time with the same quality.** Develop-then-lock-in releases in 7 days instead of 13.2, with the same number of defects left for customers (0.39) and 4 engineer hours on the suite instead of 30. The same suite costs less written once than written and rewritten throughout development.

**The suite is useful; running it in every cycle is slow.** Running the suite in every cycle, on top of testing in place, does remove defects: 0.33 left. But each cycle takes twice as long. Waiting for the experts to find nothing new for longer brings the same gain sooner (Figure 3, top). When the suite costs two hours a cycle instead of a day, the policies almost meet (Figure 3, bottom), as @eq-suite predicts: for these values the bound lies between three and six hours (Figure 4).

**Lock-in is not there to find bugs in the new feature.** In the simulation, one more day of expert use removes about as many defects as the lock-in day, and Figure 3 shows it. The lock-in suite earns its day later: it is what keeps the feature working through every future change. The model, which follows one feature until release, does not count that benefit. Prediction H4 does.

**Unit tests earn their place.** Without them, the loop takes a day longer at the median, because experts spend their time on crashes that a test would have caught. That is the line: keep a test that costs minutes and saves a day. Drop a test that costs a day per cycle while the feature still moves.

## 6. Predictions and a test protocol

For features built under the rule, compared with similar features built with the full suite in every cycle:

- **H1. Faster to market.** The median time from first commit to the flag being flipped for everyone falls by at least a third.
- **H2. No more escaped defects.** Customer-reported defects in the 30 days after the flip are no more frequent, within a margin fixed in advance.
- **H3. Most remaining defects are about fit (Assumption F).** Fewer than half of the defects experts find in place could have been caught by an integration or end-to-end test, as judged by someone outside the team.
- **H4. No more regressions.** The change failure rate of code *outside* the flag [@forsgren2018] does not rise, and locked-in features break no more often in the following six months.
- **H5. The experts stay engaged.** Participation and findings per expert hour do not decay over the study.

**Protocol.** Within the same teams, features are randomly assigned to one process at the start. H2 and H4 are pre-registered non-inferiority tests; H1, H3 and H5 are secondary, measured from the repository, the flag system, the defect tracker and incident logs. If H2 or H4 fails, the thesis is wrong for those teams. If H3 fails, its reasoning is wrong, even if the outcome looks good.

## 7. Objections and limitations

**"Testing in production is reckless."** Without a flag, staged rollout and rollback, it is. Here customers cannot reach the code. The real risk is the flag itself: in 2012 a trading firm reused an old flag, woke up dead code on the one server of eight that had not been updated, and lost about 460 million dollars in 45 minutes [@sec2013knight]. Flags are code. Each needs a unit test showing that, when off, the old behaviour is untouched, an owner, and a removal date.

**"Regressions in existing features."** This is the strongest objection, and the proposal does not drop that protection. Shared code is not behind the flag, so the automated regression suite of existing features runs on every build, and a failure blocks it. What goes is the per-cycle suite for the feature still under construction, not the suite guarding what customers already use.

**"Experts are not testers."** They are not meant to be. Testers know how to break software; experts know what it is for, and the loop needs the second skill. Their time is scarce. If the loop becomes an extra duty, $q$ falls and the advantage with it. It works when using the new version is part of their real work.

**"Production data is real."** Flagged features may write only what could be corrected by hand. Anything that cannot be undone goes through the thin gate. Where privacy or regulation forbids it, the loop runs on a copy of production.

**"Intent Is the Source said tests are the source."** [It did](../2026-10-21-intent-is-the-source/index.qmd), and the two papers agree. While a feature moves, unit tests state the intent. Once it is accepted, the regression suite states it for good. What goes is restating a moving intent in slow, high-level tests before anyone knows whether it is the right intent.

**Limits of the model.** It treats defects as independent and equally severe. It assumes $q$ is constant, although experts may find the obvious problems first. It does not count the value of the regression suite after release, which favours shift left in the comparison. Its parameters describe one kind of feature, so the direction of the result holds wherever @eq-suite holds, not its size. It also assumes agents really make writing and fixing fast, which the evidence for experienced developers does not yet settle [@becker2025].

## 8. Conclusion

We shifted left because a defect found late was expensive and only a test could find it early. With agents and flags, a defect an expert finds tomorrow behind a flag costs almost nothing. The defects that matter most are the ones no test plan foresees. Testing in depth a feature that is still changing slows the only loop that tells us whether we built the right thing.

Keep the checks a machine runs in minutes. Keep the automated regression suite that protects what already exists. Build each new feature behind a flag, with the people who know the domain using it every day. When they find nothing new, lock it in with a regression suite and flip the flag. Stop shifting left while you build. Test in depth when the feature is done.
